claim: Placozoans are microscopic animals adapted to extracellular grazing on biofilms.
source: As microscopic animals adapted to extracellular grazing on the biofilms over which they creep (Wenderoth, 1986), placozoans have a simple anatomy suited to exploit passive diffusion for many physiological needs
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wenderoth, 1986.

claim: Placozoans have only six morphological cell types discernible through intensive microscopical scrutiny.
source: with only six morphological cell types discernible even to intensive microscopical scrutiny (Grell and Ruthmann, 1991; Smith et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Grell and Ruthmann, 1991 and Smith et al., 2014.

claim: A greater diversity of cell types in placozoans is apparent through single-cell RNA-seq.
source: albeit a greater diversity of cell types is apparent through single-cell RNA-seq (Sebé-Pedrós, 2018a)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sebé-Pedrós, 2018a.

claim: Placozoans have no conventional muscular, digestive, or nervous systems.
source: They have no conventional muscular, digestive, or nervous systems
evidence: This is a direct statement about placozoan anatomy based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Placozoans show tightly-coordinated behaviour regulated by peptidergic signaling.
source: yet show tightly-coordinated behaviour regulated by peptidergic signaling (Smith et al., 2015; Senatore et al., 2017; Varoqueaux, 2018; Armon et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to Smith et al., 2015; Senatore et al., 2017; Varoqueaux, 2018; Armon et al., 2018.

claim: In laboratory conditions, placozoans proliferate through fission and somatic growth.
source: In laboratory conditions, they proliferate through fission and somatic growth.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of placozoan biology.

claim: Evidence for sexual reproduction in placozoans remains elusive despite genetic evidence of recombination.
source: Evidence for sexual reproduction remains elusive, despite genetic evidence of recombination (Srivastava et al., 2008) and descriptions of early abortive embryogenesis (Eitel et al., 2011; Grell, 1972)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Srivastava et al., 2008; Eitel et al., 2011; Grell, 1972.

claim: Sexual phases of the placozoan life cycle may occur only under poorly understood field conditions.
source: with the possibility that sexual phases of the life cycle may occur only under poorly understood field conditions (Pearse and Voigt, 2007; McFall-Ngai et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pearse and Voigt, 2007; McFall-Ngai et al., 2013 and involves speculation about life cycle conditions.

claim: The position of Placozoa in the animal tree proved recalcitrant to early standard-marker analyses.
source: The position of Placozoa in the animal tree proved recalcitrant to early standard-marker analyses (Kim et al., 1999; Silva et al., 2007; Wallberg et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 1999; Silva et al., 2007; Wallberg et al., 2004.

claim: Standard-marker analyses revealed a large degree of molecular diversity in placozoan isolates from around the globe, indicating the existence of many cryptic species.
source: although this paradigm did reveal a large degree of molecular diversity in placozoan isolates from around the globe, clearly indicating the existence of many cryptic species (Pearse and Voigt, 2007; Eitel et al., 2013; Signorovitch et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pearse and Voigt, 2007; Eitel et al., 2013; Signorovitch et al., 2007.

claim: Placozoan isolates show up to 27% genetic distance in 16S rRNA alignments.
source: with up to 27% genetic distance in 16S rRNA alignments (Eitel and Schierwater, 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Eitel and Schierwater, 2010.

claim: Analysis of a nuclear genome assembly strongly supported a position of Placozoa as the sister group of a clade of Cnidaria + Bilateria.
source: An apparent answer to the question of placozoan affinities was provided by analysis of a nuclear genome assembly (Srivastava et al., 2008), which strongly supported a position as the sister group of a clade of Cnidaria + Bilateria (sometimes called Planulozoa).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Srivastava et al., 2008.

claim: Placozoans have a surprisingly bilaterian-like developmental gene toolkit.
source: However, this effort also revealed a surprisingly bilaterian-like (Dunn et al., 2015) developmental gene toolkit in placozoans, a paradox for such a simple animal.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dunn et al., 2015.

claim: The largest controversy in metazoan phylogenetics has been the debate over the identity of the sister group to the remaining metazoans.
source: As metazoan phylogenetics has pressed onward into the genomic era, perhaps the largest controversy has been the debate over the identity of the sister group to the remaining metazoans, traditionally thought to be Porifera, but considered to be Ctenophora by Dunn et al (Dunn et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dunn et al., 2008.

claim: Additional studies have supported Ctenophora as the sister group to remaining metazoans.
source: and subsequently by additional studies (Hejnol et al., 2009; Moroz et al., 2014; NISC Comparative Sequencing Program et al., 2013; Whelan et al., 2015; Whelan et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Some researchers have suggested that the Ctenophora-sister result arises from artifacts such as inadequate taxon sampling, flawed matrix husbandry, and use of poorly fitting substitution models.
source: Others have suggested that this result arises from artifacts with potentially additive effects, such as inadequate taxon sampling, flawed matrix husbandry (undetected paralogy or contamination), and use of poorly fitting substitution models (Philippe et al., 2009; Pick et al., 2010; Pisani et al., 2015; Simion et al., 2017; Feuda et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Philippe et al., 2009; Pick et al., 2010; Pisani et al., 2015; Simion et al., 2017; Feuda et al., 2017.

claim: Using different sets of genes can lead to different phylogenetic conclusions, with only a small number sometimes sufficient to drive one result or another.
source: A third view has emphasized that using different sets of genes can lead to different conclusions, with only a small number sometimes sufficient to drive one result or another (Nosenko et al., 2013; Shen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nosenko et al., 2013; Shen et al., 2017.

claim: The phylogenetic controversy has spurred contemplation of possibly independent origins of several hallmark traits such as striated muscles, digestive systems, and nervous systems.
source: This controversy, regardless of its eventual resolution, has spurred serious contemplation of possibly independent origins of several hallmark traits such as striated muscles, digestive systems, and nervous systems (Moroz et al., 2014; Dayraud et al., 2012; Hejnol and Martín-Durán, 2015; Liebeskind et al., 2017; Moroz and Kohn, 2016; Presnell et al., 2016; Steinmetz et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: New sequences and analyses focusing on the position of Placozoa have been slow to emerge.
source: Driven by this controversy, new genomic and transcriptomic data from sponges, ctenophores, and metazoan outgroups have accrued, while new sequences and analyses focusing on the position of Placozoa have been slow to emerge.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on the authors' assessment.

claim: The study provides draft genomes from three putative placozoan species that span the root of this clade's known diversity.
source: Here, we provide a novel test of the phylogenetic position of placozoans, adding draft genomes from three putative species that span the root of this clade's known diversity (Eitel et al., 2013) (Table 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Table 1 and a citation to Eitel et al., 2013.

claim: Orthology assignment yielded 4294 gene trees with at least 20 sequences each, sampling all five major metazoan clades and outgroups.
source: Orthology assignment on sets of predicted proteomes derived from 59 genome and transcriptome assemblies yielded 4294 gene trees with at least 20 sequences each, sampling all five major metazoan clades and outgroups
evidence: This is a direct statement of the results from the orthology assignment procedure.

claim: From the 4294 gene trees, 1388 well-aligned orthologues were obtained.
source: from which we obtained 1388 well-aligned orthologues
evidence: This is a direct statement of the results from the alignment procedure.

claim: A set of 430 most-informative orthologues were selected on the basis of tree-likeness scores.
source: Within this set, individual maximum-likelihood (ML) gene trees were constructed, and a set of 430 most-informative orthologues were selected on the basis of tree-likeness scores (Misof et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the selection procedure with a citation to Misof et al., 2013.

claim: The 430-gene matrix yielded an amino-acid matrix of 73,547 residues with 37.55% gaps or missing data.
source: This yielded an amino-acid matrix of 73,547 residues with 37.55% gaps or missing data
evidence: This is a direct statement of the matrix characteristics.

claim: Bayesian analyses of the 430-gene matrix place Cnidaria and Placozoa as sister groups with full posterior probability under the CAT + GTR + Г4 model.
source: Our Bayesian analyses of this matrix place Cnidaria and Placozoa as sister groups with full posterior probability under the general site-heterogeneous CAT + GTR + Г4 model (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 and describes the results of Bayesian analysis.

claim: Under ML inference with the C60 +LG + FO + R4 profile mixture model, Cnidaria + Placozoa is recovered, albeit with more marginal resampling support.
source: Under ML inference with the C60 +LG + FO + R4 profile mixture model (Wang et al., 2018) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we again recover Cnidaria + Placozoa, albeit with more marginal resampling support.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: Both Bayesian and ML analyses show little internal branch diversity within Placozoa.
source: Both Bayesian and ML analyses show little internal branch diversity within Placozoa.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the results from both types of analyses.

claim: Deleting all newly-added placozoan genomes from the analysis has no effect on topology and only a marginal effect on support in ML analysis.
source: Accordingly, deleting all newly-added placozoan genomes from our analysis has no effect on topology and only a marginal effect on support in ML analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and describes the results of a sensitivity analysis.

claim: Quartet-based concordance analyses show no evidence of strong phylogenetic conflicts among ML gene trees in the 430-gene set.
source: Quartet-based concordance analyses (Zhou, 2017) show no evidence of strong phylogenetic conflicts among ML gene trees in this 430-gene set (Figure 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 and a citation to Zhou, 2017.

claim: Internode certainty metrics are close to 0 for many key clades including Cnidaria + Placozoa, indicating that support for some ancient relationships may be masked by gene-tree estimation errors.
source: although internode certainty metrics are close to 0 for many key clades including Cnidaria + Placozoa, indicating that support for some ancient relationships may be masked by gene-tree estimation errors, emerging only in combined analysis (Gatesy and Baker, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gatesy and Baker, 2005 and describes the interpretation of internode certainty metrics.

claim: Compositional heterogeneity of amino-acid frequencies along the tree is a source of phylogenetic error not modelled by even complex site-heterogeneous substitution models such as CAT+GTR.
source: Compositional heterogeneity of amino-acid frequencies along the tree is a source of phylogenetic error not modelled by even complex site-heterogeneous substitution models such as CAT+GTR (Blanquart and Lartillot, 2008; Foster, 2004; Lartillot and Philippe, 2004; Lartillot et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Previous analyses have shown that placozoans and choanoflagellates deviate strongly from the mean amino-acid composition of Metazoa.
source: Furthermore, previous analyses (Nosenko et al., 2013) have shown that placozoans and choanoflagellates in particular, both of which taxa our matrix samples intensively, deviate strongly from the mean amino-acid composition of Metazoa
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nosenko et al., 2013.

claim: Deviation from mean amino-acid composition may be a result of genomic GC content discrepancies.
source: perhaps as a result of genomic GC content discrepancies
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the cause of compositional deviation.

claim: Analysis of the Dayhoff-6 recoded matrix under the CAT + GTR model recovered full support for Cnidaria + Placozoa.
source: Analysis of this recoded matrix under the CAT + GTR model again recovered full support (pp = 1) for Cnidaria + Placozoa (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2 and describes the results of analysis on the recoded matrix.

claim: Under Dayhoff-6 recoding, the only major change is in the relative positions of Ctenophora and Porifera, with Porifera constituting the sister group to all other animals with full support.
source: Indeed, under Dayhoff-6 recoding, the only major change is in the relative positions of Ctenophora and Porifera, with the latter here constituting the sister group to all other animals with full support.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the results from the Dayhoff-6 recoded analysis.

claim: Similar recoding-driven effects on relative positions of Porifera and Ctenophora have been seen in other recent work.
source: Similar recoding-driven effects on relative positions of Porifera and Ctenophora have also been seen in other recent work (Feuda et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Feuda et al., 2017.

claim: Recoding-driven effects have been interpreted to indicate a role for compositional bias in misplacing Ctenophora as sister group to all other animals.
source: and have been interpreted to indicate a role for compositional bias in misplacing Ctenophora as sister group to all other animals
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of recoding effects in the literature.

claim: Many research groups have consistently reported strong support for Planulozoa under the CAT + GTR model using good taxon sampling and genome-scale datasets.
source: Many research groups, using good taxon sampling and genome-scale datasets, and even recently including data from a new divergent placozoan species (Whelan et al., 2017; Feuda et al., 2017; Eitel, 2017), have consistently reported strong support for Planulozoa under the CAT + GTR model.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Whelan et al., 2017; Feuda et al., 2017; Eitel, 2017.

claim: A supermatrix constructed using complete sequences of 303 pan-eukaryote BUSCOs shows full support for Planulozoa in both amino-acid and Dayhoff-6 recoded alphabets.
source: Indeed, when we construct a supermatrix from our predicted peptide catalogues using a different strategy, relying on complete sequences of 303 pan-eukaryote 'Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs' (BUSCOs) (Simão et al., 2015), we also see full support in a CAT + GTR + Г analysis for Planulozoa, in both amino-acid (Figure 3a) and Dayhoff-6 recoded alphabets (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by references to Figure 3a and 3b and a citation to Simão et al., 2015.

claim: Both the initial 430-gene matrix and the 303-gene BUSCO matrix fail posterior predictive tests.
source: Both the initial 430-gene matrix and the 303-gene BUSCO matrix fail these tests
evidence: This is a direct statement of the results from posterior predictive tests.

claim: The BUSCO matrix fails posterior predictive tests more profoundly than the 430-gene matrix, with z-scores in the range of 330–340 versus 176–187.
source: but the BUSCO matrix fails it more profoundly, with z-scores (measuring mean-squared across-taxon heterogeneity) scoring in the range of 330–340, in contrast to the range of 176–187 seen in the 430-gene matrix (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Table 2 and describes the results of posterior predictive tests.

claim: A large amount of the global difference in z-scores between matrices can be attributed to placozoans, with additional contributions from choanoflagellates and select isolated representatives of other clades.
source: Furthermore, inspecting z-scores for individual taxa in representative chains from both matrices shows that a large amount of this global difference in z-scores can be attributed to placozoans, with additional contributions from choanoflagellates and select isolated representatives of other clades (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3C and describes the results of inspecting individual taxon z-scores.

claim: At a conservative significance threshold of α = 0.10, the majority (764 genes or ~55%) of the 1388 gene set is identified as compositionally biased by a null-simulation test.
source: Remarkably, at a conservative significance threshold of α = 0.10, the majority (764 genes or ~55%) of this gene set is identified as compositionally biased by this test
evidence: This is a direct statement of the results from the null-simulation test for compositional bias.

claim: The null-simulation test for compositional bias is less prone to Type II errors than the more conventional X test.
source: This test, which compares the real data to a null distribution of amino-acid frequencies simulated along assumed gene trees with a substitution model using a single composition vector, is less prone to Type II errors than the more conventional X (Grell and Benwitz, 1971) test (Foster, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Foster, 2004.

claim: Analysis of the test-passing supermatrix shows strong support for Cnidaria + Placozoa.
source: Building informative matrices from gene sets on either side of this significance threshold, and again applying both CAT + GTR mixture models and ML profile mixtures, we see strong support for Cnidaria + Placozoa in the test-passing supermatrix
evidence: This is a direct statement of the results from analysis of the test-passing supermatrix.

claim: Analysis of the test-failing supermatrix shows strong support for Cnidaria + Bilateria.
source: and conversely, strong support for Cnidaria + Bilateria in the test-failing supermatrix (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by references to Figure 4 and its supplements and describes the results from analysis of the test-failing supermatrix.

claim: In trees built through CAT + GTR + Г4 analysis of the test-failing supermatrix, full support is observed for Porifera as sister to all other animals in both amino-acid and Dayhoff-6 alphabets.
source: Interestingly, in trees built through CAT + GTR + Г4 analysis of the test-failing supermatrix (Figure 4A,C), in both amino-acid and Dayhoff-6 alphabets, we also observe full support for Porifera as sister to all other animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by references to Figure 4A and 4C and describes the results from CAT + GTR + Г4 analysis.

claim: Analysis of the test-failing amino acid matrix under a profile mixture model recovers support for Ctenophora as sister to all other animals.
source: In contrast, analysis of this amino acid matrix under a profile mixture model recovers support for Ctenophora in this position (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and describes the results from profile mixture model analysis.

claim: For the test-failing alignment, compositional heterogeneity need not be invoked to explain why outcomes differ among analyses, as both CAT + GTR and the C60 +LG + FO + R4 profile mixture model assume a single composition vector over time.
source: indicating that, at least for this alignment, compositional heterogeneity need not be invoked to explain why outcomes differ among analyses, as some have argued (Feuda et al., 2017): both CAT + GTR and the C60 +LG + FO + R4 profile mixture model assume a single composition vector over time, but the CAT + GTR model is better able to accommodate site-heterogeneous substitution patterns (Lartillot et al., 2013; Quang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Feuda et al., 2017; Lartillot et al., 2013; Quang et al., 2008 and involves inference about model assumptions.

claim: Dayhoff-6 recoding appears impactful only for the test-passing supermatrix, where it obviates support for Ctenophora-sister in favour of Porifera-sister.
source: In the context of this experiment, Dayhoff-6 recoding appears impactful only for the test-passing supermatrix (Figure 4B,D), where it obviates support for Ctenophora-sister (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) in favour of (albeit, with marginal support) Porifera-sister (Figure 4D)
evidence: The claim is supported by references to Figure 4B, 4D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and describes the results from Dayhoff-6 recoding.

claim: Dayhoff-6 recoding diminishes support for Placozoa + Cnidaria in the test-passing supermatrix, perhaps reflecting the inherent information loss of using a reduced amino-acid alphabet.
source: and also diminishes support for Placozoa + Cnidaria (in contrast to the 430-gene matrix; Figure 2), perhaps reflecting the inherent information loss of using a reduced amino-acid alphabet for this relatively shorter matrix.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2 and involves speculation about the cause of diminished support.

claim: A possible hidden variable related to phylogenetic discordance is mean trimmed alignment length, with both the test-passing and the original 430-gene matrix composed of considerably shorter alignments than the test-failing and the 303-gene BUSCO matrix.
source: A possible hidden variable related to the phylogenetic discordance we describe, the precise significance of which remains unclear, is mean trimmed alignment length: both the test-passing and the original 430-gene matrix are composed of considerably shorter alignments than the test-failing and the 303-gene BUSCO matrix (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a statement about a potential confounding variable based on the authors' observations.

claim: Alignment length has been previously shown to be predictive of a number of other metrics of phylogenetic relevance.
source: Indeed, alignment length has been previously shown to be predictive of a number of other metrics of phylogenetic relevance (Shen et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shen et al., 2016.

claim: The phylogenetic link between cnidarians and placozoans seen in gene sets less influenced by compositional bias will require further testing with other analyses and data modalities.
source: The previously cryptic phylogenetic link between cnidarians and placozoans seen in gene sets less influenced by compositional bias will require further testing with other analyses and data modalities, such as rare genomic changes
evidence: This is a statement about the need for further validation of the findings.

claim: Many workers presume that placozoans must have a still-unobserved, more typical development and life cycle, or else are merely oddities that have experienced wholesale secondary simplification.
source: Many workers, citing the incompletely known development (Eitel et al., 2011; Pearse and Voigt, 2007) and relatively bilaterian-like gene content of placozoans (Srivastava et al., 2008; Eitel, 2017), presume that these organisms must have a still-unobserved, more typical development and life cycle (DuBuc et al., 2018), or else are merely oddities that have experienced wholesale secondary simplification, having scant significance to any evolutionary path outside their own.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies and describes a common view in the field.

claim: Much work on cnidarian models in the evo-devo paradigm is predicated on the notion that cnidarians and bilaterians share many homologous morphological features.
source: Indeed, it is tempting to interpret this new phylogenetic position as further bolstering such hypotheses, as much work on cnidarian models in the evo-devo paradigm is predicated on the notion that cnidarians and bilaterians share, more or less, many homologous morphological features, viz. axial organization (Genikhovich and Technau, 2017; DuBuc et al., 2018), nervous systems (Liebeskind et al., 2017; Moroz and Kohn, 2016; Kelava et al., 2015; Kristan, 2016; Arendt et al., 2016), basement-membrane lined epithelia (Fidler et al., 2017; Leys and Riesgo, 2012), musculature (Steinmetz et al., 2012), embryonic germ-layer organisation (Steinmetz et al., 2017), and internal digestion (Presnell et al., 2016; Putnam et al., 2007; Hejnol and Martindale, 2008; Martindale and Hejnol, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The authors hesitate to dismiss placozoans a priori as irrelevant to understanding early bilaterian evolution, as they have equal status to cnidarians as an immediate extant outgroup.
source: While we do not argue, as some have done (Schierwater, 2005; Syed and Schierwater, 2002), that placozoans resemble hypothetical metazoan ancestors, we hesitate to dismiss them a priori as irrelevant to understanding early bilaterian evolution in particular: although apparently simpler and less diverse, placozoans nonetheless have equal status to cnidarians as an immediate extant outgroup.
evidence: This is a statement of the authors' perspective on the significance of placozoans, with citations to Schierwater, 2005; Syed and Schierwater, 2002.

claim: The authors see value in testing assumed hypotheses of homology by extending pairwise comparisons between bilaterians and cnidarians to include placozoans.
source: Rather, we see value in testing assumed hypotheses of homology, character by character, by extending pairwise comparisons between bilaterians and cnidarians to include placozoans
evidence: This is a statement of the authors' perspective on future research directions.

claim: Recent progress has been made in reducing the disparity in knowledge between placozoans and other taxa using methods such as in situ hybridization, image analysis, and single-cell RNA-seq.
source: an agenda which demands reducing the large disparity in embryological, physiological, and molecular genetic knowledge between these taxa, towards which recent progress has been made using both established methods such as in situ hybridization (DuBuc et al., 2018) and image analysis (Varoqueaux, 2018), as well as new technologies such as single-cell RNA-seq (Sebé-Pedrós, 2018a; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2018b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to DuBuc et al., 2018; Varoqueaux, 2018; Sebé-Pedrós, 2018a; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2018b.

claim: Characters that can be validated as homologous between Bilateria and Cnidaria must have originated earlier in animal evolution than previously appreciated.
source: Conversely, we emphasize another implication of this phylogeny: characters that can be validated as homologous at any level between Bilateria and Cnidaria must have originated earlier in animal evolution than previously appreciated
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic position of placozoans.

claim: Homologous characters between Bilateria and Cnidaria should either cryptically occur in modern placozoans or else have been lost at some point in their ancestry.
source: and should either cryptically occur in modern placozoans or else have been lost at some point in their ancestry.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic position of placozoans.

claim: Paleobiological scenarios of early animal evolution founded on phylogenetically-informed interpretations of Ediacaran fossil forms and molecular clock estimates may require re-examination.
source: In this light, paleobiological scenarios of early animal evolution founded on inherently phylogenetically-informed interpretations of Ediacaran fossil forms (Cavalier-Smith, 2018; Cavalier-Smith, 2017; Dufour and McIlroy, 2018; Sperling and Vinther, 2010; Evans et al., 2017) and molecular clock estimates (Cunningham et al., 2017; dos Reis et al., 2015; Dohrmann and Wörheide, 2017; Erwin et al., 2011) may require re-examination.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies and involves inference about the implications of the phylogenetic findings.

claim: Haplotype H4 and H6 placozoans were collected from water tables at the Kewalo Marine Laboratory, University of Hawaii-Manoa, Honolulu, Hawaii in October 2016.
source: Haplotype H4 and H6 placozoans were collected from water tables at the Kewalo Marine Laboratory, University of Hawaii-Manoa, Honolulu, Hawaii in October 2016.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the sampling location and date.

claim: Haplotype H11 placozoans were collected from the Mediterranean 'Anthias' show tank in the Palma de Mallorca Aquarium, Mallorca, Spain in June 2016.
source: Haplotype H11 placozoans were collected from the Mediterranean 'Anthias' show tank in the Palma de Mallorca Aquarium, Mallorca, Spain in June 2016.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the sampling location and date.

claim: The stringent metagenomics binning procedure and the very low proportion of multiple orthologue hits in the BUSCO2 assessment attest to the lack of evidence for residual non-placozoan contamination within the scaffolds used for gene prediction.
source: Both the stringent metagenomics binning procedure (a procedure also expedient in other holobiont organisms (Celis et al., 2018)) and the very low proportion of multiple orthologue hits in the BUSCO2 assessment (Table 1) attest to the lack of evidence for residual non-placozoan contamination within the scaffolds used for gene prediction.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Table 1 and a citation to Celis et al., 2018, and describes quality control measures.

claim: Support for the Cnidaria + Bilateria clade can be assigned to compositional heterogeneity as a source of systematic error.
source: We demonstrate that a majority of genes show evidence of compositional heterogeneity, and that support for the Cnidaria + Bilateria clade can be assigned to this source of systematic error.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's findings regarding systematic error.

claim: It is possible to obtain strong support for either a sister-group relationship between Cnidaria and Placozoa, or for Cnidaria and Bilateria, depending on the orthologues selected to construct the matrix.
source: Using site-heterogeneous substitution models, we show that it is possible to obtain strong support, in both amino acid and reduced-alphabet matrices, for either a sister-group relationship between Cnidaria and Placozoa, or for Cnidaria and Bilateria as seen in most published work to date, depending on the orthologues selected to construct the matrix.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's main finding.
